Messages.Author: Synesios
Messages.Body:
Collusion is covered under the "Cheating" section (5.1, under
Tournament Violations). All cheating situations are to be reviewed and
penalized by the Head Judge, but it is all that is required to be done.
Not that I don't like the solution taken; in fact, I'm a fan of
preventing things from occuring instead of correcting them later. The
seating is determined by the tournament organizers and need not be
exactly what the Archon proposes, so I guess there's nothing wrong in
re-arranging the tables to avoid any future charges by players.

best,

Fabio Sooner
NC for Brazil, still getting used with the little details on tournament
rules

meaningless consideration. I'm sick and tired of going to 3 or 4
table tournament and looking up in the second round and finding two
other players that I'd played with in the first round. There's no

excuse for that. NEW OPPONENTS is a much more important consideration

You are right. But in some rare situations personal judgement has to
override guidelines. Below is my statement from the german forum, explaining
the procedere in detail :

stéphane lavrut was playing a weenie cel deck. kamel was playing a !tor
embrace deck. before round 3 kamel had 1GW 5VP alas a good chance to the
final. stéphane had 0GW 0VP alas no chance to the final. stéphane (playing a
rush deck) was to be the prey of kamel, his best friend. after talking with
stéphane i came to the conclusion that stéphane would be hard pressed not to
be accused of collusion if he did anything for kamel no matter what reasons
he had. therefore i assumed that stéphane had not really a free choice how
to play the game which i considered to be a really bad situation. therefore
i swapped shane schneider (also playing a rush deck) who was also very eager
to win and in no friendly relationship to kamel with stéphane. stéphane and
kamel were happy about it because they are very honorable players and didn´t
want to have an aire of collusion around them. all the other players on
these two tables were asked and agreed to the solution, sascha neumayr was
the only one who didn´t agree at first but could be convinced that it is a
good way to handle the situation.

this wasn´t (of course) a gift because neither kamel nor stéphane took a
game win in that round and for no one the situation improved/got worse. of

course i wouldn´t have anticipated the very likely case of a problematic
situation if i didn´t know them so well, but i would have suggested the same
procedere if you and one of your friends were in the same situation.

of course this change is recorded in the archon and therefore will be part
of the official report going to Robyn. there isnt any section in the vekn
rules that state anything about this but on the other hand there is no
section that states that someone has to use the archon seating charts to
determine seating.

--
johannes walch

Messages.Author: James Coupe
Messages.Body:
In message <con4k3$ceh$1...@stu1id2.ip.tesion.net>, Johannes Walch

<johanne...@vekn.de> writes:
>after talking with
>stéphane i came to the conclusion that stéphane would be hard pressed not to
>be accused of collusion if he did anything for kamel no matter what reasons
>he had. therefore i assumed that stéphane had not really a free choice how
>to play the game which i considered to be a really bad situation.

Make sure that players know they are free to call "you" (or another
judge, if appropriate to that tournament) over at any point, and that
extra time will be allocated where lengthy discussions are needed to
deal with[0] difficult allegations of collusion and similar. Re-iterate
this wherever it might be pertinent.

It doesn't matter if they're *accused* of collusion. What matters is
whether or not they're colluding in reality. Since, as judge, you'll be
required to rule in any event of collusion, this isn't really any
different. You know as a judge that some/many tricky rulings will come
up, and some will be controversial.

Going back over time, we've certainly had allegations of (say) French
people giving assistance to other French players at a table. (I do
recall French examples being given in the past, but there is no
particular reason for picking France other than that.) Should you set
it up so that they don't ever sit together? If you'll stop one set of
allegations of collusion coming together but not another potential set,
it's a very tricky line you walk. You leave the position of Judge open
to criticism of intervening arbitrarily which detracts from your own
authority.

To be honest, were it me handling this, I'd be much happier hovering
over a problem table when not circling the rest of the game, to see how
it goes. I've often hovered near a table that's - for example - got
several new players on it in order to try and prevent minor errors
occurring.

[0] Ask for details, go over the history, get other input, discuss with
other players and so on.

--

In a 3+F tournament? You can't sit with more than 12 (before the
finals). :-) I'm not sure if you meant to write "14 other players",
talking about a 3-table tournament, or if you meant that you'll sit with
more than half of them if it's a less-than-25-player tournament.

In a 15-player tournament, for example, it looks like you get 9 or 10
other players to sit with over 3 rounds.

In a 13-player tournament, though, it's sometimes only 7 different
players over 3 rounds (though the maximum would have been in that case
10, due to sitting at 4-player tables twice - for some players it's 8
versus a maximum of 11, sometimes 8 out of 10), and two are often
repeated from the first round to the second. This is probably because
of the "equalize 4 versus 5 player table seating as much as possible"
criteria for the charts, as Scott said.

In an 18-player tournament, um, wait. It looks like the chart has
player 14 on a 4-player table all three rounds? That can't be right.
:-) This appears to be on account of player 3 being on a 5-player table
all three rounds; I guess one of the 3s should swap with one of the 14s.

Let me go on to use the 17-player chart as an example instead. :-)
Players here get 9 out of 10, or 8 out of 10, or 8 out of 9 possible
opponents, it looks like.

So yeah, in smaller tournaments, probably you're going to repeat at
least one opponent at least once, and sometimes you annoyingly have to
play against two previous opponents at the same time. But you will at
least play against mostly new opponents - 70% of the most new opponents
possible, at worst, I think. (For tournaments with at least 3 tables.)

Josh
